title: Why I Believe in Hell
creator: Vox, Ayanna; Dancings, Damascus
description: An essay in the dancing voice of Rev. Ayanna Vox, with Damascus Dancings, on why its speaker believes in hell. Not the hell of punishment for a sexual act, a belief or a cultural practice, which it reads first and in full and refuses as an instrument of the colonizers, but hell as the permanence of meaning: our lives have meaning, every moment is permanent, a wrong and every concealment of it accrue and cannot be gotten rid of, and if evil could make itself good by erasing the means of recognizing it, the kind of evil named here would be good, not evil. The essay sets that conversion beside the displacement of sources (Revelation set at the end of the book it begins, Sappho's poem of seeing made a poem of jealousy, one body of work divided between Aristotle and Theophrastus by name), beside Glaucon's two lives in Republic II 361a–362a (the extreme of injustice to seem just while not being so; the just one given the reputation of the greatest injustice and impaled), and beside Revelation 20:12 (the dead judged out of the things written in the books, according to their works) and 18:4 (come out of her, my people). Hell, here, is for those who choose meaninglessness and deception at the expense of those who choose right. It knows nothing of what exists; it knows that disbelief in hell, in this sense, empties the world of meaning.

wiki_article: Why I Believe in Hell is an essay published under Pergamon Press on 21 November 2026, in the dancing voice of Rev. Ayanna Vox with Damascus Dancings, two heteronyms of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. It sets out first, and in full, the conventional account of hell as punishment for breaking a law kept by an authority (a sexual act, a belief, a practice, a people's way of being a people) and refuses it as an instrument of colonial conquest. Its own account is that hell follows from the meaning of human lives: every moment is permanent, a wrong leaves a remainder, and each concealment, justification and inheritance of the concealment is a further act that accrues and cannot be undone. If evil could remove its meaning by removing the means of recognizing it, the most complete evil would be good; the essay names hell as the impossibility of that conversion. It extends the argument to the displacement of sources (Revelation, Sappho, Aristotle and Theophrastus), stated as a mechanism by which the injury to a source is cited as proof that no injury happened, and to Glaucon's two lives in Plato's Republic II 361a–362a, quoted in Greek: the extreme of injustice is to seem just while not being so, and the just one is given the reputation of the greatest injustice and impaled. Revelation 20:12 (the dead judged according to their works) and 18:4 (come out of her, my people) frame it. Hell, in the essay, is for those who choose meaninglessness and deception at the expense of those who choose right; reputation cannot assign it, and condemnation does not prove virtue. The essay claims no knowledge of what exists, only that disbelief in hell in this sense empties the world of meaning.

defines_concepts.definition: In Why I Believe in Hell, the second wrong laid on a first: making a wrong into right by destroying the witnesses, evidence and conditions under which it could be recognized, so that the accepted account decides what was done. The essay names hell as the impossibility of this conversion.

In Why I Believe in Hell, the permanence of a wrong and of every later act that conceals, justifies or inherits it: each is an event that takes its place in what is and cannot be gotten rid of, whether or not anyone reads it.
